title: Jewellers Face Higher Hallmarking Costs as Festive, Wedding Demand Picks Up
excerpt: The BIS raised the gold hallmarking fee 67% to Rs.75 per article from September 14, just as buying season begins — and jewellery stocks slid on the news.
body:
• The Bureau of Indian Standards raised the gold hallmarking fee 67% to Rs.75 per article from Rs.45, effective September 14, under the BIS (Hallmarking) Amendment Regulations, 2026.
  • Silver hallmarking is unchanged at Rs.35 per article, and minimum consignment charges stay at Rs.200 for gold and Rs.150 for silver.
  • Jewellery shares fell on September 16: Kalyan Jewellers and PC Jeweller dropped 4-5%, while newly listed Lalithaa Jewellery Mart hit a 5% lower circuit.
  • The flat fee bites hardest on lightweight jewellery — exactly what is selling more as elevated gold prices push buyers toward smaller pieces and exchanges — and the industry body GJC has urged BIS to review the hike.

India's jewellers are heading into the festive and wedding season with a new compliance cost. The Bureau of Indian Standards has raised the hallmarking fee for gold articles by 67% — to Rs.75 per piece from Rs.45 — effective September 14.

What changed

The increase was notified through the BIS (Hallmarking) Amendment Regulations, 2026, dated September 14, which replaces Schedule IV of the BIS (Hallmarking) Regulations, 2018. Under the amended schedule, jewellers pay Rs.75 per gold article to recognized Assaying and Hallmarking Centres, subject to a minimum charge of Rs.200 per consignment. The fee the centres themselves pay to BIS for gold articles rose proportionally, from Rs.4.50 to Rs.7.50 per piece.

Silver is untouched: the hallmarking charge stays at Rs.35 per article with a Rs.150 minimum consignment fee. Hallmarking verifies the purity of precious metals in jewellery; certified articles carry the BIS logo, the karat or millesimal fineness marking, and a six-digit Hallmark Unique Identification (HUID) code.

Why the timing stings

The hike lands just as buying season begins — and it lands unevenly. Elevated gold prices have pushed consumers toward lighter jewellery and exchanges, making the flat per-article fee more significant for lower-value pieces. A one-gram pendant and a heavy bridal necklace attract the same Rs.75 charge.

Amit Modak, chief executive and director of Reva Diamonds by P.N. Gadgil & Sons, said the arithmetic changes at scale. 'The Rs.30 increase per article may appear small in isolation, but when multiplied across the large number of articles that an organized retailer hallmarks, it becomes a meaningful incremental cost,' he said.

'The Rs.30 increase per article may appear small in isolation, but when multiplied across the large number of articles that an organized retailer hallmarks, it becomes a meaningful incremental cost.'

— Amit Modak, CEO and Director, Reva Diamonds by P.N. Gadgil & Sons

Modak suggested a lower fee slab for articles below a certain weight to address the disproportionate impact on small earrings, rings and pendants, with the threshold decided through consultation among BIS, industry and other stakeholders. Supriya Kataria, founder of Mumbai-based Kumari Fine Jewellery, said her company would charge customers the notified fee at actuals without adding a margin, calling hallmarking 'a statutory consumer protection fee that directly assures purity and HUID traceability.'

Markets react, industry pushes back

Investors moved quickly. On September 16, Kalyan Jewellers and PC Jeweller fell around 4-5%, while newly listed Lalithaa Jewellery Mart touched its 5% lower circuit. The central question for shareholders is whether jewellers pass the higher compliance cost to customers or absorb it — a decision that could shave margins in a quarter when volumes matter most.

The All India Gem and Jewellery Domestic Council (GJC) has urged BIS and the government to reconsider. GJC chairman Rajesh Rokde said the industry has consistently supported mandatory hallmarking, but questioned the rationale for raising the per-article charge by nearly two-thirds at a time when hallmarking volumes have expanded enormously — and asked that the existing charge be retained pending stakeholder consultation.

Diaspora angle

For the diaspora, the change lands squarely in wedding and festive buying season, when many NRIs purchase gold in India. The fee itself is tiny next to the price of gold — but for buyers of lightweight everyday pieces, it adds a fixed layer of cost that did not exist a week ago, and it gives jewellers one more input to manage in their pricing.

What's next

Watch whether BIS engages with the industry's review request — and how organized retailers handle the pass-through question through Diwali and the wedding season. If volumes hold despite the higher fee, jewellers will absorb the noise; if lightweight demand softens, expect the push for a weight-based slab to gain force.
